items.title: Share price and intrinsic value can diverge for years
items.claim: Robert Shiller's work (Nobel 2013) showed stock prices vary much more than fundamental dividends would justify. What's the implication for share price as a measure of company performance?

options.text: Share price always equals intrinsic value at all times
Share prices can diverge from intrinsic value for extended periods (excess volatility); managers focused on quarterly share prices may make worse long-term decisions
Share price has no link to fundamentals ever
Only private firms have intrinsic value

items.reveal_title: Markets price emotions as well as cash flows
items.reveal:
Shiller's 1981 American Economic Review paper showed S&P 500 prices fluctuated 5-13x more than dividend-based fair value would justify. Tech bubble peaks (2000, 2021) and crisis troughs (2009, 2020) bookend this excess volatility.

Warren Buffett quotes Benjamin Graham: 'In the short run the market is a voting machine, in the long run a weighing machine.' Managers paid largely in stock options can be incentivised to manage the voting machine rather than build long-term weight.
items.why: Headline share price moves often reflect investor sentiment as much as company performance. Compensation and strategy that anchor on share price import this volatility.

items.title: SWOT analysis is often misused as a sorting exercise
items.claim: SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) emerged from Albert Humphrey's work at Stanford in the 1960s-70s. What's the standard critique?

options.text: It is a complete strategic plan
SWOT identifies factors but provides no method to translate them into strategy; without TOWS-style cross-pairing (S-O, S-T, W-O, W-T), it's just four bullet-point lists
It can only be used for new ventures

items.reveal:
Heinz Weihrich's 1982 TOWS matrix paired Strengths with Opportunities (offensive strategies), Strengths with Threats (defensive), Weaknesses with Opportunities (improvement), and Weaknesses with Threats (mitigation).

The core SWOT critique is that without this step, the framework lists factors without forcing a strategic choice. Most student SWOTs stop at the list stage — which is descriptive, not strategic.
items.why: SWOT looks like analysis but often delivers sorting. The strategic value is in the combinations across quadrants.

items.title: Taylor's piece rate was an incentive, not a wage
items.claim: F.W. Taylor at Bethlehem Steel in the 1890s introduced piece-rate pay. What was the central design feature?

options.text: All workers received the same base pay regardless of output
Workers were paid per unit produced, with the 'scientific' target set so only those following Taylor's prescribed method could earn the bonus
Piece rates were determined by union negotiation

items.reveal_title: Pay per piece, conditional on method
items.reveal:
Taylor's pig-iron handling experiments at Bethlehem Steel (1898-99) raised loading from 12.5 to 47 tons per worker per day. Workers earning the bonus received about 60% more pay; the firm got 280% more output per worker.

Unions opposed Taylorism fiercely — 1911 US Congressional hearings investigated 'speed-up' abuses. Modern piece rates persist in garment factories, gig economy (Uber surge pricing as a variant) and sales commissions.
items.why: Piece rates align effort with output but can erode quality, safety and worker autonomy. The same design principle reappears in 'pay for performance' compensation a century later.
